speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head P of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These include agents of influence, funding, hacks and leaks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, according to a report to the United States (US) Senate, Russia twitter bots seemed to have been involved in Brexit through social media.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not to be taken lightly as interracial tensions were escalated by foreign state actors in the case of the US that is deepening the black-white divide.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: State actors were allegedly behind the Macron hack and leaks, where forged emails were mixed with real ones and were released at the 11th hour.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the Centre for International Governance Innovation, protection of critical infrastructure, such as voting machines and voter registry, are important to prevent and protect against foreign interference of the democratic processes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the past five years, there has been an upward trend in the amount of cyber threat activity against democratic processes globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may be hard to detect as false accounts and groups that originated from a foreign country can pose as local, as was done during the mid-term elections in the US.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we must guard against such threats descending on and vesting in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we add muscle to our legislative framework and regularly update the regulatory machinery to preserve and protect domestic policymaking as the rightful domain of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What can we learn of the modus operandi of foreign pressure groups, overt and covert, that have insurrected the policymaking and legislative spheres of other countries?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a study will assist our Home Team to deter such modus operandi from being deployed here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point is this, that to preserve the effective and efficient running of Singapore, and to ensure our system of governance is not undermined by ill-minded external forces, we need to add more muscle to our armoury of legal weapons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A study of insurrectionist fake news movements around the globe show that hostile information campaigns are deployed in an attempt to undermine institutions, social cohesion and trust in governments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As effectiveness and efficiency can be hampered by an unabated spreading of untruths, the need for Singaporean security agencies to detect and counter them is crucial for the longevity of our system of governance and its continued efficiency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, to protect Singapore's reputation as a safe country in which systems of governance, trade and industry function predictably and effectively, we should have an armoury of legal tools to combat propagators of fake news and the ill consequences of their trade.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is important that this armoury of legal tools be versatile, as disinformation campaigns have become even more sophisticated and we need to keep up with the advancements in techniques of concealment and manipulation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For example, in a Politico article, it stated that "fake news merchants are a step ahead" of government efforts, challenging the definition of what constitutes fake news through the use of photo-based disinformation and the use of Internet messaging services like WhatsApp, as well as employing techniques to mask their locations and purchase of political ads in local currencies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Every 21 July, Racial Harmony Day is celebrated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The first series of riots in the Race Riots of 1964 began on 21 July.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Those riots had been called "the worst and most prolonged in Singapore’s postwar history".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But the fact that we can celebrate Racial Harmony Day is a testament of how much stronger our unique social fabric has grown.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Unique Singapore is made up of many races – Malay, Chinese, Eurasian, Indian and groups of other ethnicities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Along with the ethnicities, there is a wide representation of religions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Through the Ethnic Integration Programme, people of different races live side-by-side.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, with the rise of inflammatory speech around the world seeking to incite violence against people based on religion or race, what are our ongoing plans to further safeguard our racial and religious harmony?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A United Nations (UN) expert stated that there is a "dramatic" increase in the number of websites and social media platforms that enable the incitement of violence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Tackling the social media aspect is important, as words on social media can quickly go viral like a fire which is out of control.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This can be done through the use of bots.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Of particular concern to me is the "slow drip" effect, as some falsehoods may play on existing "slow burn" issues, such as simmering communal tensions, to create more serious crises in the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have seen social media being used to spread inflammatory messages that could cause tension among different communities and to share hate speeches.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These conversations are then carried into the real world and can affect the way we interact with one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The online space is also used to spread practices which may not be compatible with our local context.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sometime back, news broke about several foreign preachers being banned from preaching in Singapore for this reason.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, religious harmony is vital for peace and prosperity in our multiracial and multi-religious nation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Over the years, the Government and religious community have made great strides in safeguarding our religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We have continuously affirmed the need to foster a culture of mutual understanding and the attitude of live and let live, as well as to build strong bonds among different faiths.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Building and maintaining religious harmony are an ongoing effort since our Independence, and we cannot be complacent.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Even though these segregationist ideologies may not cause immediate harm, like violence, they can divide society over time.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I urge the Government to work more closely with our religious communities to take steps to prevent such segregationist tendencies from taking root in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MHA share its plans to do so?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These marriages would have a strong and sustainable Singaporean Core to begin with, and even more so, when these married couples decide to start a family.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these foreign spouses may be in their second marriage and have children of their own with them.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While these foreign spouses may be granted permanent residency in due course, their children from previous marriages are facing an uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These children will not get Permanent Resident (PR) status by default.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In such cases, Singaporeans with foreign stepchildren to raise would have to struggle with non-subsidised school fees, medical fees and more, if they are unable to legally adopt these children.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For example, to adopt a stepchild from China, the consent of the biological ex-spouse must be sought.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If the ex-spouse is missing, non-cooperative or even hostile, it is next to impossible for the Singaporean to legally adopt his stepchild.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these stepchildren can never go back to their home countries as well because they were abandoned at birth by one half of their parents.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Here, we have children who are already an integral part of the Singaporean Core families, who are totally integrated into our society and who are as Singaporean as any one of their local siblings.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These grown-up children can then make their own declaration to become citizens at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In my conversations with Singaporeans with foreign stepchildren, they are deeply concerned how their stepchildren would feel as they grow older and come to know that they are actually quite different from their brothers or sisters in many ways.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I urge the Ministry to grant these stepchildren of families with a strong Singaporean Core, permanent residency or citizenship sooner rather than later.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increasing global threats posed by terrorism, cyberattacks and international crimes, this move is timely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The growth of new technologies poses a growth of new threats.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat, in his Budget speech, said that this year, digital defence has been incorporated as the sixth pillar that makes up Singapore's Total Defence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MHA share more on the plans for the new agency and how it will help enhance the capabilities of the Home Team?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With digitalisation and advances in technology, what is the Home Team doing to leverage technology to enhance operations, service delivery and address the constraints faced with manpower?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will the new agency use technology and information offensively and defensively?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To be effective in prevention of, response to and recovery from cyberattacks, it will require interagency coordination.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Other agencies, like the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Heath, are required in the research and development of homeland security technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In what way is MHA fostering and driving interagency cooperation and coordination?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is MHA doing to attract the right talent and developing security specialists for the agency?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We know that cyber terrorism has no boundaries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The private sector also makes investment in technology for security and hence private sector partnership can also strengthen the use of technology for homeland safety.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MHA share what public, private, national and international partnerships the new Science and Technology Agency intends to drive in researching, developing and sharing homeland security technologies?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If the agency is the extension of the current work of the Science and Technology office to pre-empt and contain terrorist attacks, that is a good development.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, I am concerned with the scope of surveillance and profiling technology to be deployed and developed.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Sometime ago, the Minister for Home Affairs said that the integration of facial recognition technology into the Home Team information technology (IT) systems could help automate Police work.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Recently, many organisations, including tech giants, such as Microsoft and Google, have raised alarm on facial recognition and its potential abuse if left unregulated.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Some critics have pointed to China's misuse of the technology for political control.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How will the Government ensure that the data collected is authentic, is secured and not subjected to abuse, political or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What safeguards are there to ensure that the privacy and rights of citizens will not be violated?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What recourse will citizens have to address possible misuses of personal data and violations of privacy by the Home Team?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An effective way to nurture and strengthen religious harmony is to make sure that people from different religions interact with one another.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in recent times, we have seen overseas examples of segregationist behaviour.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, there were media reports about laundromats in Malaysia only wanting to serve Muslim customers and extremist Buddhist monks in Myanmar calling Buddhists to boycott Muslim businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to make sure that such separation of people based on religion is not acceptable here.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Reducing social mixing among believers of different religions will divide our society over time and splinter our nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we ensure that such segregationist practices do not take root in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In view of the volume and increasingly serious nature of digital threats, a dedicated agency will boost our Home Team's technological capabilities to provide greater support for its operational needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The range of cases which our security agencies have to deal with are getting more diverse and more complex by the day.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cyberattacks and cybercrimes are escalating even as general crime rates are stabilising or falling.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will it interface with other similar agencies, such as the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA)?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Chairman, the world we live in is very different from the past.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Through the porous and interconnected Internet, crime and threats of unrest can be caused by players beyond a country's borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Even within Singapore, the medium of the Internet provides a cover that can easily mask one's identity and location.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Nevertheless, what is on the Internet can have consequences in real life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As such, combating falsehoods, protecting race and religion from speech inciting violence, ensuring domestic politics and sensitive policy decisions remain the domain of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These are all key and important facets to our way of life and the continued effectiveness of our rule of law governance system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Science and technology can be studied and deployed to detect foreign and domestic actors who seek to spread falsehoods and incite violence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As experts have stated, this is important as there are cyber armies in the region that can be easily deployed against Singapore directly or as proxies for another country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This can also include civilians who unwittingly participate as circulators of disinformation or even as part of a "militia" that acts in support of a state-sponsored disinformation campaign.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Will the new MHA arm in the form of the Science and Technology Agency work to deploy the disciplines of science and technology to deter disinformation or information that incites violence and instability?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP) colleague once made an appeal on behalf of a member of the public who lives in a constituency he contested in General Election 2015.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am, therefore, surprised as to why the SPF acknowledged the appeal from PAP Party Branch Chairman, whereas the appeal from an NCMP was not accepted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, our officers will encounter more complex and sophisticated cases while frontline officers, such as those in the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), will encounter heavier workloads and ever higher service expectations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister update on the progress of the project, especially how it has impacted our ICA and Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While technological changes have made law enforcement more complex for our Home Team officers, it also heralds the dawn of ever more effective officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Law enforcement has evolved, from the physicality of beat patrolling to remote advanced monitoring and detection systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our older officers can be trained to take on different but equally productive work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How have we redesigned our jobs to take advantage of technology to help our officers to be productive even when they are older?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How are we also reskilling our officers so that they can better utilise technology in their work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the face of manpower constraints and increasing workloads, we must necessarily help officers to work better for longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Law enforcement officers are like fine wine – they get better with age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their legal knowledge and contextual experience are important in sniffing out suspicious cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many successful Police and ICA arrests are due to the skills of our officers built up over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage MHA to leverage assistive technology and changes in job scopes and law enforcement methodologies to extend the retirement and re-employment age of our Home Team officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In an increasingly complex operating terrain, we no longer have the monopoly of knowledge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our officers often know what are the skills that they need to thrive in the environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will the Ministry consider setting up training committees comprising ground officers, senior management and headquarter staff in our various land divisions to explore new skills and new ways to train?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As an example, one need only refer to the amendment Bill to the Penal Code that was tabled in Parliament earlier this month.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If passed, it will introduce a slew of new offences to better protect the more vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: SPF will also have to ensure it has the resources to deal with security issues to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How much can technology really be leveraged to free up manpower, given that there will always be a limit to what can be done without the human touch?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: One can even purchase cannabis-flavoured drinks, cookies and ice-cream in nations where their recreational use has been legalised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: However, the damage of such drug misuse on our health is undeniable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: And I urge the Government to prevent this trend from taking root in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I am also very worried about how the abuse of such drugs will lead to the exploration of and subsequent addiction to other illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What is the Government’s stance on this issue and how does it plan to respond to this growing trend globally?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What measures do we have to ensure that such illegal drugs do not find their way into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Calls to decriminalise the consumption of highly addictive and illicit drugs should be viewed with scepticism and suspicion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These calls have an agenda, as some of those voicing them have much to gain financially.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, if we were to decriminalise the supply and demand of drugs, who suffers the social fallout?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Who has to pave the road to recovery of a citizen addicted to drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Who has to care for the family broken by a member’s drug addiction?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Who suffers as a result of drug-related crimes?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Certainly, not the big industries seeking to profit from liberal drug consumption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rather, it is the family of the drug addict that suffers the most – an innocent spouse, child or baby – and, of course, the state.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, we must deter both the demand and supply of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What then is MHA's position regarding moves to make cannabis legal in neighbouring countries?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Separately, what steps are being taken to increase the employability of former rehabilitated addicts?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, there is a growing trend globally and regionally to legalise cannabis for recreational and medical use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In October 2018, Canada became the second country in the world to legalise cannabis for recreational use, after Uruguay became the first such country in 2013.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the US, around 10 states have legalised cannabis for recreational use and more than 30 states have legalised cannabis for medical use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In our region, two countries have recently legalised cannabis for medical use – South Korea in November 2018 and Thailand in December 2018.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This trend poses implications for young people, patients and healthcare professionals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Young Singaporeans studying or working in jurisdictions which have legalised cannabis may have attitudes towards drugs shaped by the social environment there.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Patients in Singapore may read online posts about jurisdictions which have legalised cannabis for medical use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthcare professionals, in turn, may be faced with challenging conversations with patients, who might ask about differing policies regarding legalisation of cannabis for medical use, across different countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What is the Government’s assessment of this emerging trend in overseas jurisdictions?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has always taken a tough stance against drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For drug traffickers, the death penalty may even be imposed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This policy stance takes into account the potential damage and detrimental effects that drug abusers cause themselves, their families and the wider Singaporean community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not think that this belief has changed over the years amongst the majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The recent numbers for 2018 released by the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), however, reveal a worrying trend.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Drug abusers in the 20-29 age group continue to form the largest group of abusers in 2018.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister to share with this House further details of the Ministry’s plans to reduce the number of youths involved in the consumption of drugs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: (In Malay):   Earlier this year, I had the opportunity to join Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin in one of the outreach events for the Dadah Itu Haram campaign at the coffee shops within Bukit Batok as well as Changi Village.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We joined several other volunteers, including representatives from the Singapore Muslim Women's Association (PPIS), to walk the ground and convey the anti-drug message to the shopowners and their customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such efforts are a good platform to get to know the community and obtain feedback.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Through the session with Mr Amrin Amin, I found that, generally, many people are aware of this campaign and our community’s efforts to combat drugs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I realise that a lot of time and effort have been spent on this campaign and it appears to be successful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Although there is now a deeper understanding of the importance of staying away from drugs and numerous efforts to help drug abusers rehabilitate, there is still some concern about the number of Malay/Muslim abusers compared to other communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Drugs do not only affect the abuser, but also the drug abuser’s family and children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The effort to combat drug abuse in our community must continue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, I would like to ask for further details about the Dadah Itu Haram campaign.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What was achieved over the course of the campaign?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Has there been any effort to measure its effectiveness?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Are there other plans to enhance public education about these anti-drug efforts so that we can see a reduction in the number of drug abusers or a decline in the drug problem within our community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In concert, the drugs of choice have also evolved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, psychoactive substances and methamphetamine are the norm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the recent amendments to the Misuse of Drugs Act in the direction of rehabilitation for hardcore addicts are to be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the surface of things, it would appear that they would have fewer obstacles procuring drugs as compared to low-income addicts who may resort to crime to feed their urge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a prospect may mean that hardcore addicts with criminal antecedents and para-criminal charges would ironically have lesser access to the new rehabilitation regime which can help keep them out of long-term detention.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A useful indication of how the new regime may operate would be to have some sense of the income and social economic background of hardcore addicts who are under the LT regime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to enquire if there is a distinction to the type of drugs consumed by low-income and affluent addicts respectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I urge the Ministry to keep a tab on this issue to see how low-income hardcore addicts can be better rehabilitated since many, in view of the concurrent criminal record of antecedents, may not be able to extricate themselves out of the LT regime towards rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Paradoxically, these low-income hardcore addicts may need the most help and rehabilitative assistance.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Chairman, when offenders are released from the prisons, many leave with a desire to change, to reconnect with their families and to contribute to the community.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Securing employment is a critical step for ex-offenders to start afresh.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Having and being able to keep a job gives one a sense of purpose and self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It also gives one meaning and satisfaction from being able to provide for their family and themselves.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, the transition from prison to work is not easy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: With limited work experience or the gap from previous work experience and some with low or no educational qualifications, many inmates may only be able to qualify for entry-level positions when they re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For many individuals, the fast-changing labour market is a concern.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This is especially challenging for ex-offenders as they must adapt to a job environment that may have changed from the time when they went into prison.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Employers’ support for ex-offenders in the workforce is key to enhancing inmates' employability.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I have met several ex-offenders at my Meet-People-Session asking for help to find a job, and because of not being gainfully employed, they have to seek financial assistance to help their daily needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, our prison takes a rehabilitative approach towards ex-offenders and, as such, there are a number of programmes to rehabilitate and reintegrate offenders so that they may become responsible citizens upon completion of their sentence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for rehabilitation to be successful, they must first have a safe place to stabilise their lives, or they could risk falling back to crime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of my residents started sleeping at the void deck of his flat for months shortly after his release from prison.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He had no one to turn to and was completely lost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He came to my Meet-the-People Session for food rations and help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am concerned for those who thought they had a home to return to, but only to find that their family was not willing to accept them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They did not want to go back to get a referral, or they found the process to be troublesome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then there are also those who do not like the interim housing options because of the restrictions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of my residents told me they prefer staying with friends who would have them, or in public places until they have found a stable job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, many job applications would require the applicant to give their home address, so this poses another stumbling block for this group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry and other relevant agencies establish a hotline and safe lodging coupled with job agency services to help these people get back on their feet?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What more can MHA and the prisons service do to ensure the prisoners have the necessary fallback option if the homes they return to are not viable?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can more be done in terms of resources by MHA and other national agencies to ensure inmates have a hotline or safe lodging for them with a comfortable environment and embedded job search agency services for these groups of people before they stabilise their lives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can MHA and relevant agencies also work with the private sector real estate agencies and/or property agents to ensure the supply of adequate matching of rental housing is available for inmates about to be released or have been released but found out they have emergency housing issues?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, while the number of fires that occurred last year has fallen, more than half of them occurred in residences with more people injured in fires last year suffering from burns and smoke inhalation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In 2018, there were four fatalities from fires and all cases occurred at home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In our constituency at Changi Simei, there were three residential fires in 2018, two occurred during the charging of PMDs and another involved a fish tank catching fire.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Two weeks ago, a fire broke out in the switch room of Carlton Hotel.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I was actually having lunch at the hotel and was amongst the thousand people that had been evacuated from the premises.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Fortunately, there were no injuries, but the fire did cause power disruptions for nearby buildings and several Mass Rapid Transit stations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With our dense population, high-rise buildings, close living proximity and work environments, how can we improve fire safety for our buildings, especially older buildings?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How can we ensure the readiness of our people to know what to do to stay safe in the event of a fire?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, SCDF designated residential buildings that go beyond 40 storeys as Super High-rise Residential Buildings.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: There are additional Fire Code requirements, such as the creation of refuge floor with holding area at 20-storey intervals and the installation of larger capacity fire lifts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In 2013, such buildings were required to have two fire lifts to facilitate the evacuation of people with disabilities by firefighters.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The Competent Person, such as the Managing Agent’s supervisor, will perform fire safety duties and train security guards to execute evacuation procedures properly.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In a fire at a 48th floor unit at Pinnacle Duxton in May last year, it was reported that a man and a woman in their 60s were hurt, suffering smoke inhalation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It was also reported that many residents living on the 47th and 48th floors chose to use the lifts to evacuate despite knowing the risk of being trapped in the lifts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: There is urgency in this with the ageing society, as more and more seniors find it onerous to walk down 20 storeys to the refuge floor.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Some seniors may not even know that they should not evacuate using the fire lifts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The efforts taken in SG Secure to create awareness in the community and equip people with skills to respond to crises like terror attacks are commendable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The awareness on the ground of the importance of preparedness has been enhanced over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is still some room though to develop the actual preparedness, for example, by encouraging more people in the community to go through training for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and on the use of automated external defibrillators.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could be coupled with efforts to build racial and religious understanding amongst the different communities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At the international platform, we hear about the strength of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) waning.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, there are still instances of self-radicalisation occurring all around the world and, in particular, in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We, therefore, need to continue being vigilant and continue to "exercise those muscles" so that we remain prepared.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The efforts in creating awareness and preparedness must continue as we learn lessons from incidents abroad and reflect on the instances of self-radicalisation in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Could MHA provide an update on the efforts carried out so far and the plans for SGSecure moving forward, as well as MHA's efforts in combating self-radicalisation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: So far, Singapore has been fortunate in that we managed to avoid major incidents, thanks to the diligence and competence of our security agencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Besides boosting security measures, we have to strengthen our ability to deal with the consequence of potential attacks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Our community must remain united across ethnic and religious groups.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Minister share updates on SG Secure and how it would help to foster a community which is more resilient and self-reliant in dealing with crises like terror attacks, as well as MHA's efforts in combating self-radicalisation?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christoper de Souza, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While we put in place steps to deter terror threats, we must, equally, be prepared in the event a threat vests on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not just the prevention of terror attacks that counts but the "cure" after it happens.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Even as we currently enjoy racial and religious harmony, we cannot take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A concrete sense of resilience must prevail in the minds of all Singaporeans, regardless of race or religion, to remain united, steadfastly protecting the racial and religious harmony while rejecting the threat of terror and its perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What steps has MHA taken to detect and deter self-radicalisation and what community-based exercises will be carried out to imbue a sense of post-attack resilience in fellow Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Cybercrimes may have a transnational element to them, but their ill consequences can be felt harshly at home.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is especially when syndicates target the elderly in cheating cases or when love scams are deployed to take advantage of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To stem the harm felt in Singapore, my question is: how will MHA build on its capabilities to tackle local and cross-border cybercrimes and enhance public awareness to help prevent their re-occurrence?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Chairman, traffic accidents are regrettable occurrences on our roads.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In Singapore, we legislate strong measures to minimise the number of traffic accidents.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In an ideal world, all traffic accidents should be prevented.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In the meantime, it is clear that certain road user behaviours directly increase the risk of traffic accidents that could potentially result in injuries or fatalities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Instances, such as drink driving or running a red light, are two examples.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Traffic accidents arising out of these reckless and irresponsible driving behaviors are avoidable and should be sternly dealt with as these drivers put not only themselves, but other road users at risk.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Some of the numbers recently released by MHA on the road traffic accident situation for 2018 raises serious concerns about such reckless and irresponsible driving behaviours.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It has been reported that MHA is already taking steps to impose stiffer penalties for drink-driving and other road traffic offences.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I invite the Minister to share with this House if the Ministry is considering taking any other steps, such as further raising awareness amongst the public or the imposition of a review course requirement, for responsible driving on new or experienced drivers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Top reasons cited in the survey were more aggressive drivers and non-drivers on the road.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Based on recent media reports, while the number of accidents has fallen, there is an upward trend in irresponsible driving.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What are the causes for irresponsible driving in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Some reports have alleged that texting while driving is worse than driving drunk in its effect on your ability to drive safely, as it splits your attention.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What actions are taken to address dangerous driving situations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And how will the Home Team further improve road safety to make our roads safer for all road users?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, in New Zealand, for young drivers, there is a zero-alcohol limit imposed against them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In many states of Australia, zero-alcohol limits are also imposed on probationary drivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It seems to me that the regulations are imposed not because young and probationary drivers are more likely to drink-drive compared to other drivers, but because there is a need to better protect them from the effects of alcohol which is likely to impair their judgement much more than the experienced and older drivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The average number of drink-driving arrests per year is 2,298.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Whilst the instances of drink-driving amongst probationary and young drivers in Singapore are relatively low, the numbers are not piffling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: More importantly, our laws do not make a distinction on the impact of alcohol on probationary and young drivers’ judgement as compared to other experienced drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Twenty-eighteen was an intense year for the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: High-signature events – the Trump-Kim Summit, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit because we were the Chair of ASEAN, and, of course, some issues arose in our waters from the disputed Malaysia Johor Port Limits.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, to deal with that, the Police Coast Guard has been operating at a very high tempo since when the dispute began, round the clock.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the entire Home Team, because of the events of last year, has been working round the clock.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I want to thank all the Home Team officers for their hard work, their dedication and the professionalism with which they have approached their work.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Like in past years, we continue to rank very highly on indices on safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The crime and drug situations remain under control and our internal surveys, which we do regularly, show that public trust and confidence in the Home Team remain extremely high.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The approach for the new Science and Technology Board is to deepen the Home Team's scientific and engineering capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to strengthen the operational effectiveness and work on developing new technologies, focusing on threat detection, digital forensics, unmanned systems.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Really, it will pool together Science and Technology (S&T) resources, integrate S&T requirements across the Home Team, and attract and develop S&T talent, which is critical.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Minister Josephine Teo will speak in more detail about our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will also update the Committee on other plans to maintain Singapore's safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin will speak on drug abuse prevention, rehabilitation of offenders, cybercrime and the Home Team manpower transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling will speak on improving fire and road safety and also improving community partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will speak on two emerging concerns, which Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Baey Yam Keng, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have raised: one, foreign interference in domestic politics; and second, trends that may undermine our religious harmony and what we intend to do about both of these.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will also speak about the rehabilitation of low-income drug abusers, a point raised by Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last month, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong spoke on overseas examples of foreign interference in domestic politics and elections.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Members and the public know the impact that foreign interference has on politics in different countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hostile information campaigns have been used to weaken countries' resolve when countries are in conflict or tension between states where one country uses hostile information campaign to destabilise the other country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Foreign actors have attempted to undermine democracy and elections in a number of countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Foreign interference has also come into play to try and weaken the social fabric of different countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about the need to look at what has happened to other countries, how they have dealt with foreign interference, and learn some lessons on what we can do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Several countries have, in fact, passed laws to combat both falsehoods as well as foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Australia, recently, legislation was passed on dealing with foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was a complete ban on foreign political donations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And those who act on behalf of foreign nations or entities must declare that relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Failure to comply could mean up to five years' jail.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And for foreign interference aimed at influencing elections or supporting foreign intelligence, people who engage in that could face a penalty of up to 20 years in jail.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The kind of penalties that you see indicate the severity of the threat and how countries are reacting to them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are studying what has happened to them and what they are doing to combat the threat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our current thinking is that early detection and exposure are critical.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we must be able to act quickly and keep up with new digital-age tactics.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, apart from strengthening our laws, we have to build up the ability of Singaporeans to understand what is happening, to discern, to respond appropriately, and to try and resist foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is a reality that many people will find it difficult.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of the steps that I have outlined can only be taken through legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Member said that recent changes to the Misuse of Drugs Act may inadvertently operate in favour of drug abusers who come from more affluent households, and are we are doing enough to help low-income hardcore addicts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That data shows that those in the lowest 20th percentile of wage earners are no more likely to have both drug and criminal convictions at the same time, as compared to those who earn more.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will be eligible to be channelled to DRCs if they admit to drug use and have committed no other crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is an answer based on the facts in the current situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Take a situation where there are those who abuse drugs and those who abuse drugs as well as committed crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those who abuse drugs, the right thing to do is not to look so much at their economic or social background, but to see what is going to help them kick the habit and become useful citizens in society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And our approach, based on many years of data and experience, science- and evidence-based, is that we can do more with rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, let us take those who commit crime in addition to abusing drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is in their interest that we help them both to kick their drug habit and, at the same time, not commit a crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is also to prevent them from committing a crime and ensuring the safety of society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, those on the second category need to be helped to move out of criminality and drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we try and achieve that through a number of programmes, when they are in detention.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How to help them, whether in LT or DRC, stay off drugs and crime is something that we are intensely focused upon.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And hopefully, with our programmes, regardless of which socioeconomic group they come from, when they come out, they are able to lead a healthy life and a more productive life from their own perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, for example, we have put in place a range of programmes to address the varied and complex causes of both addiction and crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, for all drug abusers, Prisons provide psychology-based correctional programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members can understand, Mr Singh can understand, if you committed a crime, you have done this, you go in, you get access to psychology-based correctional programmes which I think they need to address their underlying drug addiction issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They also undergo skills training and work programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, we find that for those who, when they come out, are able to keep a job, their recidivism rate is much lower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we have to help them while they are in prison to try and get the right attitudes towards getting and keeping a job.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also partner the community, such as halfway houses and religious organisations, to provide various forms of support, for example, interim housing arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, those with a higher risk profile of re-offending are given more help, through the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, after they get released, they go through the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our intention is to try and make it work and we will make further changes where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members spoke about them or asked what the Government's response is.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will identify three trends that are of concern.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, resurgence of identity politics around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: More people are identifying themselves in narrow ethnic, cultural and religious terms.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They turn inwards, they reject diversity, they reject co-existence with others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Political parties and movements that ride this wave have gained traction around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, far-right parties have made electoral gains in France, the Netherlands and Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Alt-right movement gained prominence in the US as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Significant support for religion-based parties and parties which advocate moves in this direction have gained in our immediate region as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng spoke about increasing segregationist ideas and practices.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can come from foreign preachers, they can come from the Internet.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One particular example of such teaching is what was said in Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ashin Wirathu – some Members may be familiar with him – urging Buddhists to boycott Muslim businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I quote, "do business or interact with only our kind: same race and same faith".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is all around us, and he is not alone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second worrisome trend, as Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have noted, the Internet has allowed hate speech and incitement to spread further and faster, and there can be devastating effects.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The third trend is religiously-motivated terrorist groups who continue to spread their propaganda.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Overseas experiences show that in the immediate aftermath of a terror attack, there is distrust, there is suspicion between communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the rise of Islamophobic incidents in Paris and Brussels in wake of attacks would be known to Members.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Christopher de Souza asked how we should respond.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, of course, the non-"sexy" bit as it were, is what we have always been doing, that is, continue to build a strong Singaporean identity, preserve and grow our common space and experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a lot of work and it takes a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we are where we are here today because of all the steps that we have taken over 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our education system, public housing and National Service, all examples of us coming together, common space, people of different backgrounds, understanding, creating our own value system, and building common experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we have to continue to keep religion and politics separate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have managed to balance the right to religious freedom, with a secular approach to politics, and with the need to ensure harmony, peace and security in our multiracial, multi-religious society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A key challenge – it is an increasing challenge – is to ensure that we can maintain the right balance in the face of the challenges that Members have spoken about that I have acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, we have to preserve the culture of mutual respect for one another’s religions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to reach out across religious lines and keep the avenues of conversation open.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, of course, the Government is a key player and partner in this process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I will focus on the Home Team’s efforts to use science and technology to safeguard Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team is in the midst of an ambitious multi-year effort to transform itself to remain effective and capable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members would be familiar with the challenges confronting the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While ISIS has lost most of its territory in the Middle East, it remains a potent threat, inciting attacks in our part of the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We continue to see cases of self-radicalisation in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Criminals are employing more sophisticated tactics with the help of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We see this in the rise of cybercrime and online scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The workload of the Home Team has continued to increase and public expectations are rising.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To cope with these challenges, simply increasing manpower is neither sustainable nor effective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The way forward is for the Home Team to change the way we do things.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Ms Jessica Tan pointed out rightly, technology will enable us to be effective, even in the face of manpower constraints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our borders are Singapore’s first line of defence against security threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Protecting our borders is no easy feat and will only get more challenging.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, we need to rely on technology to meet these challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One way to do so is through biometrics technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This system will allow ICA to use a combination of any of the three biometric identifiers, namely iris, facial and fingerprints, for immigration clearance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This paves the way for a more efficient and secure immigration clearance process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: BioScreen-MMBS will provide our officers with a more dynamic tool to accurately identify travellers, especially those who could be of security interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will also allow ICA to build a robust biometrics database comprising the face, fingerprints and iris of every individual who crosses our borders, for post-incident investigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Technology is critical not only to combating threats at our borders, but also inland.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first is in detection, sense-making and surveillance capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From major security incidents abroad, we know that a strong, immediate and coordinated response is key to saving lives, neutralising threats and restoring order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have invested heavily in surveillance, command-and-control, and sense-making capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, our Police Operations Command Centre uses real-time video feeds and data to enhance incident response.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Already, our installation of Police Cameras (PolCams) in public areas has effectively deterred crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Surveillance capability is also critical for identifying and apprehending terrorists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) used surveillance footage to identify the perpetrators of the Boston Marathon bombing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Photos of the suspects were released within days of the bombing to help the public locate them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have plans to further strengthen our detection, tracking and sense-making capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Video analytics will allow the Home Team to rapidly track down criminals and terrorists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Joint operational dashboards and common situation pictures will enable us to deliver more coordinated responses to incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Police are exploring the digitalisation of forensic data, and building intelligence into forensics systems, to improve their sense-making and analytical prowess.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Digital forensic laboratories will enhance our ability to extract evidence from digital devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These capabilities will go a long way in enabling the Home Team to rapidly generate leads and to apprehend offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third area is in robotics and unmanned systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to strengthen and augment our physical force and presence using robotics and unmanned systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), give ground commanders a bird’s eye view of the operating terrain and enhance their situational awareness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Robots can help firefighters tackle large-scale fires more effectively and safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Robots and UAVs will eventually be able to carry out even more complex tasks autonomously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will play a greater role in surveillance, search and rescue operations and in dealing with hazardous materials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman and Members, I have spoken about some of the important capabilities that support the Home Team’s current operations and that help to keep security threats at bay.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we know that we are heading into a future where science and technology will play a bigger part.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have to up the game in order to keep Singaporeans and Singapore safe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA has thus far partnered other Government agencies, such as the Government Technology Agency (GovTech), the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) and the Defence Science Organisation, as well as industry partners like ST Engineering and Singtel, to develop these capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are currently ramping up our collaboration and partnership with these and other partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, MHA will work with GovTech more closely in the area of ICT and digital services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And DSTA will help MHA to develop future command and control systems and new marine platforms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as we look to further leverage technology, we will need to set up a dedicated agency to further develop the Home Team’s science and technology capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Why is a dedicated agency going to be able to do that better?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, many of the capabilities I have spoken about, such as forensics, biometrics and surveillance, will become increasingly critical to safeguarding Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, many of these capabilities are unique to the Home Team, reflecting our distinct operational context and mission requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Like other countries which have dedicated technical agencies for homeland security, the Home Team needs to strengthen our core team of scientists and engineers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, a dedicated agency will boost the joint Home Team approach, with capabilities developed and shared across Departments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Lastly, centralising science and technology talent that is today distributed across the different Home Team departments will better support career development for the officers, which, in turn, deepens organisational capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ultimately, to combat fast-evolving security threats and to safeguard Singapore, the Home Team must possess deep inhouse capabilities and expertise to build mission-critical abilities in a responsive manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will be responsible for developing and sustaining capabilities to support Home Team Departments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To achieve this, the agency will conduct applied research and develop new systems to be deployed in the Home Team’s various operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the scientists and engineers of this new agency, technical expertise is necessary, but not sufficient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They must also have a deep understanding of the Home Team’s unique operational needs, in order to apply and integrate effective solutions, and to work alongside Home Team officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will be part of the Home Team, so that we can build capabilities in a timely and responsive manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And I look forward to the debate in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I welcome Members' views and contributions when we table the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang asked an important question about data security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is, of course, an issue that is very much on our mind, especially as the use of technology and data becomes more prevalent across the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, there are already strict guidelines on how data is collected, accessed, stored and protected in the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, sensitive data can only be accessed by authorised officers who have a legitimate purpose for doing so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are also systems in place that help to track and monitor what data was accessed or modified by whom, to guard against abuse and to ensure that data collected is authentic and secure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: You can find out who made what modifications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And if we find out that something was done, we will take disciplinary action.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA takes its responsibility as the custodian of the data it collects very seriously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We, of all agencies, understand that any data abuse, breach or leak can severely compromise public trust.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, if you will allow me, I would like to conclude in Mandarin.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, in the coming years, science and technology will become increasingly indispensable in the Home Team’s efforts to combat security threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will help to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe and secure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is of utmost importance that we plan ahead to ensure that our Home Team officers have the full support they require to exploit technology to our advantage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A new dedicated science and technology agency for the Home Team will give us the much needed expertise and focus to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am confident that the Home Team will succeed in its mission to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Chairman, I will focus on four areas: fighting cybercrime and scams; transforming the Home Team; keeping Singapore drug-free; and supporting rehabilitation and reintegration of offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On the first area, fighting cybercrimes and scams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Last year, crimes reported increased by 1.4%, largely driven by an increase in scams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The public continues to fall largely for three types of scams: e-commerce scams, such as online purchase scams; two, credit-for-sex scams, where scammers pose as attractive women on social media platforms; and, three, China officials' impersonation scams, where victims receive calls from seemingly official numbers, and are told to provide banking details or remit money to assist in "criminal investigations".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Last year, one victim lost about $1.7 million this way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about how MHA would be tackling cybercrime, especially those targeting the elderly and Internet love scams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: First, we have strengthened international cooperation with foreign law enforcement agencies to disrupt foreign syndicates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In 2017, Police set up the Transnational Commercial Crime Task Force to investigate cross-border scams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Police also set up the E-Commerce Fraud Enforcement and Coordination Team in November last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: There is a dedicated scam advisory hotline and "Scamalert.sg" website which provide information on the latest scams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have worked with online marketing platform Carousell, convenience stores, remittance agencies, banks and other stakeholders to remove suspicious advertisements, publish scam advisories, and look out for potential scam victims.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: To educate the elderly who are vulnerable to such scams, the Police conducted Silver IT Fest 2018.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The Police also reached out to elderly residents through home visits and Silver Watch, a programme to equip seniors with crime prevention knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Together with the National Crime Prevention Council, we launched the "Let’s Fight Scams" campaign, partnering community and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will continue to focus on this fight.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Chairman, turning now to my second area – Home Team Transformation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: MHA has embarked on Home Team Transformation since 2015.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The Transformation aims to strengthen joint operations in the Home Team, deepen our science and technology capabilities, and upskill our officers to better meet future challenges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about how MHA would ensure that SPF would be sufficiently resourced to continue to operate effectively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: SPF is constantly looking at new ways to improve productivity and efficiency of our officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: As part of the Home Team Transformation, systems are developed to support ground operations and ease administrative workload.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: One example is SPF's convenient and citizen-centric e-Services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On 8 July 2018, the revamped e-Services 1.0 was introduced.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Members of the public can now perform online transactions, such as reporting crimes, from home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Self-help terminals have also been installed at several Neighbourhood Police Centres.
